title: Prototype crate skeleton with the complete candidate registry
description:
A new `dev/research/permanent_wave_gpu/` crate created with its candidate registry already complete, so the study's arithmetic and kernel candidates can be implemented concurrently without any two of them editing the same file.

## Background

The wave-parallel permanent study implements five GPU candidates over $\mathbb{F}_3$, $\mathbb{F}_5$, and $\mathbb{F}_7$, several of them at the same time. A crate whose module list and dispatch registry grow one entry per candidate would put every candidate on the same two files, so the registry is created complete instead: every planned candidate is enumerated from the start, each entry dispatching to a named function in that candidate's own module, and each of those functions begins as a stub returning an unsupported result with a stated reason.

That is the harness's single-list backend schedule applied to a crate. A registered path cannot silently miss a measurement cell, and a path that cannot run is recorded with a reason rather than dropped, which is how the existing measurement harness already represents a backend it cannot execute.

The build plumbing follows the same rule. Compiling an enumerated list of kernel sources would put every candidate back on the build script, so the build script compiles whatever HIP sources it finds under the crate's `hip/` directory — the way the in-tree per-architecture blob pipeline collects its own sources. A no-op probe source keeps that path exercised before any candidate kernel exists, mirroring the probe source the kernels crate generates for the same reason.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: `dev/research/permanent_wave_gpu/` exists as a standalone crate outside the default Cargo workspace, carrying a `.gitignore` whose entries are `target/` and `Cargo.lock`.
- [hard] REQ-02: The crate README states the crate's scope, its build and test invocations, and the registry convention by which a candidate is implemented.
- [hard] REQ-03: The crate's module list and measurement-path registry enumerate the study's full planned candidate set, so a measurement driver enumerates every planned path from the start and implementing a candidate later requires no edit to either registry file.
- [hard] REQ-04: Each registry entry dispatches to a named function in that candidate's own module file, and each such module file exists with that function returning an unsupported result carrying a stated reason.
- [hard] REQ-05: A test enumerates the registry and asserts that every planned candidate is addressable and that an unimplemented one reports unsupported with a reason rather than panicking or returning a value.
- [hard] REQ-06: The build script compiles every HIP source found under the crate's `hip/` directory rather than an enumerated list, so adding a kernel source needs no build-script edit.
- [hard] REQ-07: A no-op probe HIP source keeps the device compile path exercised while no candidate kernel exists, and the build succeeds on a ROCm host with only that source present.
- [hard] REQ-08: `cargo test --manifest-path dev/research/permanent_wave_gpu/Cargo.toml --release` passes on a host with no device.
- [hard] REQ-09: `cargo fmt --manifest-path dev/research/permanent_wave_gpu/Cargo.toml -- --check` and `cargo clippy --manifest-path dev/research/permanent_wave_gpu/Cargo.toml --release --all-targets -- -D warnings` report no findings.

## Notes

Scope is the crate skeleton, its registry, and its build plumbing. Fixtures, the oracle comparator, and candidate implementations land against this skeleton afterwards.

The crate is excluded from the default workspace, so the workspace CI pipeline never compiles it; the explicit `--manifest-path` invocations above are the only build evidence for this change.

Crates under `dev/research/` are permanent repository content, which is what lets rejected candidates and their falsifying evidence stay compiled and tested for the life of the study.

planning.outcome: A standalone prototype crate exists with the full planned candidate set registered, each entry reporting unsupported until implemented.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: A crate skeleton with one registry file and five stub modules is mechanical work verifiable in a single focused cycle without a device.

title: Deterministic fixture corpus with CPU-oracle equivalence checking
description:
A deterministic seeded fixture corpus and a CPU-oracle equivalence checker in the study's prototype crate, which every arithmetic and kernel candidate is measured against before any timing counts as evidence.

## Background

The study compares arithmetic representations and GPU execution mappings for permanents over $\mathbb{F}_3$, $\mathbb{F}_5$, and $\mathbb{F}_7$. No correctness evidence is admissible until a candidate is shown exactly equal to an in-tree CPU oracle on inputs that reach the structural boundaries of the algorithm, not only on uniform random matrices.

The existing measurement harness at `dev/research/permanent-sampling-feas/` samples uniform random matrices only. Nothing in the repository constructs matrices or Gray-code indices that target a range boundary, an addition-versus-subtraction transition, a nonzero exponent class, or a zero-containing row product. That corpus is prerequisite infrastructure for the candidate work rather than a rider on any single candidate.

The oracle is `gf2_algebra::permanent::permanent_ryser`, which is field-agnostic and asserts $n \le 63$, so it covers every order the study measures, including orders where no packed $\mathbb{F}_7$ kernel exists. Where a packed scalar kernel supports the order, it serves as a second reference and the reference actually used is recorded per row.

The horizontal product of a row-packed Ryser step takes its slow path only when every active row sum is nonzero, and takes its zero fast path otherwise. For a uniform random matrix and a fixed nonempty column subset the row sums are independent and uniform, so with $Z$ the active zero mask,

$$
\Pr[Z = 0] = \left(\frac{q-1}{q}\right)^n
\quad\text{(slow path)},
\qquad
\Pr[Z \ne 0] = 1 - \left(\frac{q-1}{q}\right)^n
\quad\text{(zero fast path)} .
$$

The two expectations are complements, and an observed frequency is only interpretable against the one matching its own path.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A fixture module emits a deterministic corpus keyed by an explicit seed, so that two runs at the same seed produce byte-identical matrices, and the corpus is reproducible from a committed command.
- [hard] REQ-02: The corpus covers, for each of $\mathbb{F}_3$, $\mathbb{F}_5$, and $\mathbb{F}_7$: empty and singleton matrices where the exercised API accepts them, Gray-range boundary indices including the first and last index of a partitioned interval, both addition and subtraction Gray transitions, active-lane masking at partially filled words, zero-containing row products, and each nonzero exponent class of $\mathbb{F}_q^*$.
- [hard] REQ-03: The corpus includes orders $n = 16$, $n = 20$, and $n = 24$ for $\mathbb{F}_7$, spanning the $n \le 16$ bound that the current 16-lane packed $\mathbb{F}_7$ representation imposes.
- [hard] REQ-04: An equivalence checker compares a candidate's per-matrix result element-wise against `gf2_algebra::permanent::permanent_ryser`, reports the count of mismatching matrices together with the first mismatching fixture identifier, and records a candidate that cannot execute with a stated reason instead of dropping it.
- [hard] REQ-05: The checker reports, for each $(q, n)$ cell of the corpus, the observed zero-fast-path frequency beside its exact marginal expectation $1 - \left(\frac{q-1}{q}\right)^n$ and the observed slow-path frequency beside $\left(\frac{q-1}{q}\right)^n$, stating that the two expectations are complements.
- [hard] REQ-06: The checker is reached through the crate's existing measurement-path registry, so it admits any registered candidate without an edit to that registry.
- [hard] REQ-07: `cargo test --manifest-path dev/research/permanent_wave_gpu/Cargo.toml --release` passes, exercising the corpus against the oracle through the CPU-side reference paths.

## Notes

The prototype crate is excluded from the default workspace, so the workspace CI pipeline never compiles it; the explicit `--manifest-path` invocation above is the only build evidence for this change.

The value-to-exponent tables the exponent-class coverage is drawn from are, with generator $2$ for $\mathbb{F}_5$ and generator $3$ for $\mathbb{F}_7$:

| $\mathbb{F}_5$ value | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $3$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Exponent | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |

| $\mathbb{F}_7$ value | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ | $6$ | $4$ | $5$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Exponent | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ |

planning.outcome: A seeded fixture corpus reproduces exact CPU-oracle permanents across the study's boundary classes for three fields.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One fixture module and one oracle comparator dropped into an existing crate skeleton, all host-side, fits a single focused cycle.

title: HIP event timing API for device-side kernel spans
description:
A HIP event wrapper in the kernels crate's device host layer, returning the elapsed device time of a kernel span so a measurement can separate kernel execution from allocation, copy, and host serialization.

## Background

Every GPU figure recorded for the permanent kernels so far is a wall-clock span around a whole dispatch: host serialization of the batch, two device allocations, a host-to-device copy, the launch, a device synchronize, a device-to-host copy, and two frees. Kernel-only duration cannot be recovered from it, and no HIP event is used anywhere in `crates/gf2-kernels-hip` today.

Event objects are device resources acquired and released through the HIP FFI, which is the same category as the buffers, streams, and launch dimensions the crate already owns. `crates/gf2-kernels-hip/src/host/` exports `DeviceBuffer`, `PinnedHostBuffer`, `HipStream`, `HipStreamPool`, and `LaunchDims`; events belong beside them. The crate reaches the HIP runtime through one raw-ABI path — thin `extern "C"` shims in `hip/host_runtime.hip` with their Rust declarations in `src/ffi.rs`, the way the stream and allocation infrastructure is bound today — and the event entry points enter through that same path rather than through a second binding mechanism. A private event helper inside a research crate would duplicate a shared device-resource mechanism, which the repository's convention-convergence rule treats as a defect unless it is a named exception.

One event pair is also not enough on its own. A dispatch is four distinct spans — the host-to-device copy, the kernel, the device-to-host copy, and the launch interval around the submission — and a study that reports transfer cost separately from kernel cost needs all four from a single run rather than from repeated runs with pieces removed. The API therefore records a phase-tagged sequence of event spans across one dispatch.

Launch overhead needs one more rule, because the obvious definition is unsound: the interval between a host-side enqueue timestamp and the kernel start event subtracts a host timestamp from a device timestamp, and a difference across two clocks is not a duration. The boundary instead reports two quantities, each on its own clock — the host-side duration of the submission call itself, and the device-only elapsed time from a marker event recorded on the launch stream at submission to the kernel start event — and never combines them arithmetically.

An event pair alone also does not isolate kernel time here. The permanent dispatchers launch on the default stream and call a device-wide synchronize inside the dispatch, so a caller bracketing that call measures the synchronize rather than the kernel. Isolating the kernel needs a launch boundary that records the start and stop events on the launch stream around the kernel itself and returns without a device-wide sync, leaving the caller to await the stop event. That boundary is part of this work.

The boundary also cannot be built on the kernel entry points as they stand: every permanent kernel entry point hard-codes the default stream — `hipLaunchKernelGGL(…, /*stream=*/0, …)` in each of the three `hip/permanent/permanent_bipedal*.hip` sources — so no caller-supplied stream can reach a permanent kernel today. Stream-bearing variants of the batch launch entry points, taking a `hipStream_t` through the FFI, are part of this work; the existing entry points keep their behaviour by delegating to the variants on the default stream.

The existing dispatch entry points keep their current synchronous contract: production callers are unaffected, and the instrumented boundary is an additional surface rather than a change to the shipped one.

This is production `unsafe` in the crate that is permitted to hold it, so each FFI boundary carries its own safety contract.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: `crates/gf2-kernels-hip/src/host/` exposes an event type that acquires a HIP event on construction and releases it on drop, with no path that leaks the event on an error return.
- [hard] REQ-02: The event entry points — create, destroy, record, query, and elapsed time — are bound through the crate's existing raw-ABI path, as `extern "C"` shims in `hip/host_runtime.hip` with declarations in `src/ffi.rs`, each declaration carrying its safety contract, with no second binding mechanism introduced.
- [hard] REQ-03: The API records a start event and a stop event on a caller-supplied stream and returns the elapsed device time between them in milliseconds.
- [hard] REQ-04: Querying elapsed time before the stop event has completed returns a stated error rather than a partially observed duration.
- [hard] REQ-05: Every `unsafe` block the change introduces carries an explicit safety contract naming the precondition it relies on.
- [hard] REQ-06: An event-instrumented launch boundary records the start and stop events on the launch stream around the kernel and returns without calling a device-wide synchronize, so the reported duration covers the kernel rather than the enclosing dispatch.
- [hard] REQ-07: The instrumented boundary lets the caller supply the stream it launches on, and reports the elapsed kernel time once the stop event has completed.
- [hard] REQ-08: Each permanent batch launch entry point has a stream-bearing variant that accepts a caller-supplied `hipStream_t` and launches the kernel on that stream, and the existing entry points launch on the default stream by delegating to the variants, so their behaviour is unchanged.
- [hard] REQ-09: The boundary records a phase-tagged sequence of event spans across one dispatch and returns the host-to-device copy duration, the kernel duration, and the device-to-host copy duration separately, so a caller attributes time to a phase without a second run.
- [hard] REQ-10: The boundary reports launch overhead as two separately reported quantities — the host-side duration of the submission call, and the device-only elapsed time between a marker event recorded on the launch stream at submission and the kernel start event — and no reported figure subtracts a host timestamp from a device timestamp.
- [hard] REQ-11: A phase the caller did not perform is reported as absent rather than as a zero duration.
- [hard] REQ-12: The existing permanent dispatch entry points keep their current synchronous behaviour and signatures, so a production caller observes no change.
- [hard] REQ-13: A device-gated test records a span around a known-duration kernel and asserts the returned duration is positive and strictly smaller than the wall-clock span of the enclosing synchronous dispatch of the same work.
- [hard] REQ-14: A device-gated test over a dispatch with both copies asserts that the three phase durations are each positive and that their sum does not exceed the enclosing wall-clock span.
- [hard] REQ-15: Device-touching tests are gated on the crate's `hip` feature and marked ignored with a reason naming the required device, matching the convention of the crate's existing test files.
- [hard] REQ-16: `cargo test --manifest-path crates/gf2-kernels-hip/Cargo.toml --release --features hip` compiles on a ROCm host, with the device-gated tests reported as ignored when no device is present.

## Notes

`crates/gf2-kernels-hip` is excluded from the default Cargo workspace and requires ROCm, so the workspace CI pipeline never compiles it; the explicit `--manifest-path` invocation above is the only build evidence for this change.

Scope is the event API, the stream-bearing launch variants, the instrumented launch boundary, and their tests. No measurement, receipt, or harness wiring belongs here.

planning.outcome: An instrumented launch boundary returns per-phase device durations for copies, kernel, and launch overhead in one dispatch.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One RAII wrapper over five event shims bound through the existing raw-ABI path, stream-bearing variants of the three batch launch entry points, and one phase-tagged launch boundary, each with its safety contract, is a small self-contained cycle.

title: Purpose-domain stream address allocator
description:
A bounded, injective seed-address encoding for the measurement harness, so each measurement purpose addresses the sampler through a distinct region of the seed input space instead of through a hand-chosen numeric base.

## Background

The harness derives a ChaCha20 seed from four little-endian `u64` words — campaign root, field order $q$, matrix order $n$, and a stream index — so distinct tuples address distinct generator states, and a debug assertion already catches a caller sampling one field from another field's stream label.

What the tuple does not encode is *purpose*. Which stream index belongs to which measurement activity is decided by hand-chosen numeric bases: the grid hands cell $i$ the range $1 + i \times 10^5$, and the sustained runs sit at $10^9 + j \times 10^5$. An earlier revision based the sustained runs at $10^6$, commensurate with the grid's allocation; the ranges overlapped in index space and the pooled counts were valid only because no colliding pair happened to share a $(q, n)$ — verified after the fact rather than designed. Two defects of that family corrupted a superseded result set: every sustained run started at the same stream index, so two runs at one $(q, n)$ drew overlapping matrices; and warm-up shared a stream counter with the timed repetitions, so which matrices a cell timed depended on machine speed and the recorded seed did not regenerate the recorded sample.

The study adds several measurement purposes. Minting another base for each by the same arithmetic is how that defect recurs, so the address space is partitioned by construction instead: a purpose tag occupies a fixed high-bit field of the stream word and the stream index occupies the remaining low bits, with both bounds asserted so the two fields cannot overlap.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[campaign root] --> S[32-byte seed]
    B[field order q] --> S
    C[matrix order n] --> S
    D[purpose tag in high bits] --> W[stream word]
    E[bounded stream index in low bits] --> W
    W --> S
```

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The seed derivation accepts a purpose tag alongside the existing campaign root, field order, matrix order, and stream index, and encodes that tag in a fixed high-bit field of one seed word with the stream index in the remaining low bits of the same word.
- [hard] REQ-02: The encoding asserts both bounds at the call site: a purpose tag at or above the tag field's capacity, or a stream index at or above the index field's capacity, fails loudly rather than aliasing into another purpose's address region.
- [hard] REQ-03: A test establishes that the encoding is injective over the enumerated purpose set and a bounded index range — distinct $(\text{purpose}, \text{index})$ pairs produce distinct seed inputs — so no two purposes can address the same generator state through this API.
- [hard] REQ-04: A committed table of golden derivation vectors fixes the mapping from a stated $(\text{root}, q, n, \text{purpose}, \text{index})$ tuple to its derived seed bytes and to the leading output bytes of the generator opened on that seed, so a change to the encoding fails the test instead of silently re-addressing already-committed receipts.
- [hard] REQ-05: Every measurement purpose the study runs is a named member of one enumerated purpose set, and warm-up is a distinct purpose from the timed repetitions of the same cell, so a recorded seed regenerates exactly the timed sample.
- [hard] REQ-06: Introducing a measurement purpose without giving it a tag fails the purpose-set test rather than defaulting into an existing purpose's address region.
- [hard] REQ-07: Every call site in the harness that previously computed a stream base arithmetically addresses the sampler through this encoding instead, leaving no hand-chosen numeric base in the measurement path.
- [hard] REQ-08: `cargo test --manifest-path dev/research/permanent-sampling-feas/Cargo.toml --release` passes.

## Notes

The guarantee established here is over **seed inputs**: distinct purposes and indices encode to distinct addresses, and the golden vectors pin that mapping. It is not a claim that the resulting ChaCha20 output streams are disjoint as sequences — that is a property of the cipher's construction, and no test in this work establishes it. The criteria are worded to keep those two statements apart.

Every crate under `dev/research/` is excluded from the default Cargo workspace, so the workspace CI pipeline never compiles them; the explicit `--manifest-path` invocation above is the only build evidence for this change.

planning.outcome: Each measurement purpose addresses the sampler through a bounded, injective seed encoding, with golden vectors pinning the mapping.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One bit-field encoding with its bounds assertions, an injectivity test, and a golden-vector table is a small self-contained cycle.

title: Per-phase timing columns in the harness cell record
description:
The permanent measurement harness reports event-measured kernel, transfer, and launch durations per timed cell, carried from the instrumented launch boundary through the protocol module's cell record into their own CSV columns.

## Background

Every GPU figure recorded for the permanent kernels so far is a wall-clock span around a whole dispatch: host serialization of the batch, two device allocations, a host-to-device copy, the launch, a device synchronize, a device-to-host copy, and two frees. Kernel-only duration cannot be recovered from it, and the harness's four component phases — generate, evaluate, reduce, store — offer no finer split.

Recovering it needs both halves. The device side supplies an event-instrumented launch boundary that brackets the kernel on its own stream without a device-wide synchronize; this work carries that measurement through the harness, into the protocol module's per-cell record and into the CSV schema, so a reader can tell a kernel span from a dispatch span without consulting code.

Launch overhead is two columns rather than one, because its two halves live on different clocks: the host-side duration of the submission call, and the device-only span between the submission marker event and the kernel start event. The boundary reports them separately, the record carries them separately, and no column is computed by subtracting a host timestamp from a device timestamp.

A cell whose path cannot supply an event-measured duration must say so rather than dressing a wall-clock figure as a device measurement.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The harness times each GPU cell through an event-instrumented launch boundary that brackets the kernel on its own stream, so the recorded kernel duration excludes allocation, host-to-device copy, device-to-host copy, and host serialization.
- [hard] REQ-02: The harness reports, per timed cell, that kernel-only device duration beside the existing wall-clock duration, and the CSV schema constant carries the new column so a reader can tell the two apart without consulting code.
- [hard] REQ-03: The cell record carries the host-to-device copy duration, the device-to-host copy duration, the submission call's host-side duration, and the pre-kernel device span as their own columns, each separate from the kernel duration, so a reader attributes transfer and launch cost without a second run.
- [hard] REQ-04: Host-clock and device-clock durations are distinct columns, and no column is derived by subtracting one clock's timestamp from the other's.
- [hard] REQ-05: A cell whose path cannot supply an event-instrumented duration records the affected columns as absent with a stated reason rather than repeating the wall-clock figure or writing a zero.
- [hard] REQ-06: The harness usage text describes the kernel-only and per-phase columns and the conditions under which each is absent.
- [hard] REQ-07: `cargo test --manifest-path dev/research/permanent-sampling-feas/Cargo.toml --release` passes.

## Notes

Scope is the per-phase timing columns alone. The registry-derived schedule adapter is separate work behind this leaf, sub-evaluate micro-measurements are separate work, and no campaign receipt is produced here.

Every crate under `dev/research/` is excluded from the default Cargo workspace, so the workspace CI pipeline never compiles them; the explicit `--manifest-path` invocation above is the only build evidence for this change.

planning.outcome: Each timed GPU cell reports event-measured kernel, copy, and launch durations as their own columns beside wall-clock.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: Per-phase columns threaded from the instrumented boundary through an existing protocol module and CSV schema is a single focused cycle.

title: Registry-derived schedule adapter for prototype candidates
description:
The measurement harness derives its backend schedule from the prototype crate's candidate registry through one stream-aware adapter, so the study has exactly one candidate list.

## Background

The harness and the prototype crate must not end up with two hand-maintained candidate lists that drift apart. The prototype crate carries the study's candidate registry; this work adds the adapter that derives the harness's `Backend::ALL` schedule from that registry, so a candidate registered once in the prototype crate becomes schedulable by the harness without a second list to update. Drift between two lists is silent until a cell is missing from a receipt, which is why the equality of the two sets is asserted by a test rather than by review.

The adapter is also where a candidate's stream purpose is bound, so a scheduled path draws from the purpose domain the harness assigned it rather than from one chosen at the call site.

A path registered through the adapter is scheduled by both the equivalence check and the timing grid and cannot silently miss a cell; a path whose implementation has not landed reports itself unsupported with a stated reason, which is how the harness already records a backend it cannot run.

This leaf follows the timing-column leaf on a dependency edge because the two rework the same harness files; the ordering keeps every footprint overlap on an edge and costs no wave, since this leaf's wave siblings are the field candidate leaves.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The harness derives its backend schedule from the prototype crate's candidate registry through one adapter, so a candidate registered once in that registry is schedulable without a second hand-maintained list in the harness.
- [hard] REQ-02: A candidate reached through that adapter draws from the stream purpose domain the harness assigned it, with no numeric stream base computed at the call site.
- [hard] REQ-03: A registered candidate whose implementation has not landed is reported as unsupported with a stated reason rather than omitted from the schedule.
- [hard] REQ-04: A test asserts that the set of paths the harness schedules equals the set the prototype registry enumerates, so a candidate cannot exist in one and be missing from the other.
- [hard] REQ-05: `cargo test --manifest-path dev/research/permanent-sampling-feas/Cargo.toml --release` passes.

## Notes

Scope is the schedule adapter alone. The per-phase timing columns land before this leaf on its dependency edge, and no campaign receipt is produced here.

Every crate under `dev/research/` is excluded from the default Cargo workspace, so the workspace CI pipeline never compiles them; the explicit `--manifest-path` invocation above is the only build evidence for this change.

planning.outcome: The harness's backend schedule is derived from the prototype registry through one stream-aware adapter, with set equality asserted.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One adapter module deriving the schedule from an existing registry, plus a set-equality test, is a small self-contained cycle.

title: Dependency-chained Gray update micro-measurement mode
description:
A harness mode that times one dependency-chained packed add or subtract on a single accumulator, isolated from the surrounding Ryser loop.

## Background

The study must isolate three nested measurement shapes for each arithmetic representation it measures: one dependency-chained packed add or subtract on the same accumulator; zero-mask detection plus the complete nonzero horizontal reduction; and the full Ryser loop including matrix preparation, Gray initialization, update, product, partial-sum reduction, launch overhead, and transfer overhead. The harness times the third shape and, through its per-phase event columns, separates the device spans inside it. The first two shapes have no measurement path at all.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Gray update micro-measurement] --> B[Horizontal product micro-measurement]
    B --> C[End-to-end Ryser cell]
    C --> D[Per-phase device spans inside the cell]
```

This matters because a representation decision made on bulk independent-operator throughput does not transfer to the permanent: the shipped row-packed loop performs one packed add or subtract per Gray step followed by a horizontal product over the row lanes, and it is the dependency chain through the accumulator that a permanent-shaped measurement has to expose.

This mode covers the first shape. Its defining property is the dependency chain: each packed add or subtract reads the accumulator the previous one wrote, so the measurement exposes latency rather than the throughput an independent-vector benchmark would report.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A harness mode times one dependency-chained packed add or subtract on a single accumulator, with each operation reading the accumulator the previous one wrote.
- [hard] REQ-02: The reported duration excludes surrounding loop overhead, and the method by which that overhead is excluded is stated in the mode's output.
- [hard] REQ-03: The mode reuses the committed warm-up, repetition-count, timed-duration, and censoring policy of the harness protocol module instead of defining a private timing policy, and a censored row states its censoring reason.
- [hard] REQ-04: For a GPU path the mode reports an event-measured kernel duration rather than a wall-clock span.
- [hard] REQ-05: The mode addresses the sampler through a named purpose tag drawn from the harness's enumerated purpose set, with no numeric stream base computed in the mode's own code.
- [hard] REQ-06: The mode reaches candidates through the harness's registry-derived schedule, so it covers a registered path without a schedule edit.
- [hard] REQ-07: The harness usage text describes the mode together with its arguments.
- [hard] REQ-08: `cargo test --manifest-path dev/research/permanent-sampling-feas/Cargo.toml --release` passes.

## Notes

Scope is this one mode. No campaign receipt is produced here.

Every crate under `dev/research/` is excluded from the default Cargo workspace, so the workspace CI pipeline never compiles them; the explicit `--manifest-path` invocation above is the only build evidence for this change.

title: Wave-cooperative intra-matrix Ryser prototype for F_3
description:
A HIP kernel that gives each lane of a wavefront its own contiguous Gray-code interval of a single matrix and reduces only the partial Ryser sums across the wave, for permanents over $\mathbb{F}_3$.

## Background

Every HIP permanent kernel in this repository today launches a one-thread block per matrix and runs the Gray-code Ryser walk sequentially in that thread. On an RDNA2 wavefront of 32 lanes that leaves 31 lanes inactive, and parallelism comes only from having many matrices in flight. An intra-matrix decomposition is the untested alternative: no wave-cooperative permanent kernel exists anywhere in this repository.

The study's execution mapping gives each lane its own contiguous Gray-code interval. One matrix's walk over $[0, 2^n)$ is partitioned into as many contiguous intervals as there are active lanes; each lane owns its complete packed row-sum accumulator in registers for the whole of its interval, reconstructs that accumulator from the column subset encoded by its interval's start index, applies one packed add or subtract per Gray step, and computes its own horizontal row product locally as a reduction over the row lanes inside its own packed words. Nothing is exchanged across the wave except the partial Ryser sums, which are combined in lane-index order so the reduction is scheduling-independent. The outer $(-1)^n$ factor is applied once after that reduction, and grid and block dimensions are a pure function of matrix order, batch size, and the range partition. This is `crates/gf2-algebra/src/permanent/parallel_bipedal3.rs`'s chunk model with lanes in place of rayon workers.

Giving every lane a full accumulator is what the mapping spends to buy wave utilization, so the per-lane register state and the shared column table are budgeted quantities rather than incidental ones. Beyond its packed accumulator each lane carries three scalar `u64` words — the Gray cursor, its interval end bound, and its partial Ryser sum — so the live per-lane state is the packed word count plus three. The packed column table is staged once per block from global memory by a cooperative strided copy followed by one barrier, and is read-only thereafter. Its steady-state access is **not** a broadcast: at each Gray step a lane reads the column bundle indexed by its own flip index, and flip indices differ across lanes, so shared-memory bank behaviour under that scattered read is a measured quantity rather than an assumption.

That register and shared-memory budget is the central occupancy hypothesis of the study. A packed accumulator holds a fixed number of words for any order the mapping supports, where a byte-oriented accumulator grows with $n$ and will reach scratch memory; each block additionally reserves a column table linear in $n$. Whether that budget, instruction scheduling, or the scattered shared-memory read is what limits occupancy is settled by each field's measurements, not by the estimate stated here.

That CPU precedent partitions the Gray-code index range into fixed-size chunks, reconstructs each chunk's starting column sums from `gf2_algebra::gray::gray_code_index_to_subset`, reduces the partial sums order-independently because addition over $\mathbb{F}_3$ is commutative and associative, and applies the outer factor once after the reduction.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Gray-code range of one matrix] --> B[Contiguous interval per lane]
    B --> C[Lane-local accumulator initialized from interval start]
    C --> D[Lane-local packed add or subtract per Gray step]
    D --> E[Lane-local horizontal row product]
    E --> F[Lane-local partial Ryser sum]
    F --> G[Lane-index-ordered partial-sum reduction across the wave]
    G --> H[Outer sign factor applied once]
```

Launch geometry in this repository is a pure function of problem size. A runtime occupancy query would make the launch shape depend on device state and break the pipeline's determinism contract.

Both effects are properties of the assembled kernel, so both paths have to exist as permanent-shaped kernels before either can be measured.

The study's execution mapping gives each lane its own contiguous Gray-code interval. One matrix's walk over $[0, 2^n)$ is partitioned into as many contiguous intervals as there are active lanes; each lane owns its complete packed row-sum accumulator in registers for the whole of its interval, reconstructs that accumulator from the column subset encoded by its interval's start index, applies one packed add or subtract per Gray step, and computes its own horizontal row product locally as a reduction over the row lanes inside its own packed words. Nothing is exchanged across the wave except the partial Ryser sums, which are combined in lane-index order so the reduction is scheduling-independent. The outer $(-1)^n$ factor is applied once after that reduction, and grid and block dimensions are a pure function of matrix order, batch size, and the range partition. This is `crates/gf2-algebra/src/permanent/parallel_bipedal3.rs`'s chunk model with lanes in place of rayon workers.

Giving every lane a full accumulator is what the mapping spends to buy wave utilization, so the per-lane register state and the shared column table are budgeted quantities rather than incidental ones. Beyond its packed accumulator each lane carries three scalar `u64` words — the Gray cursor, its interval end bound, and its partial Ryser sum — so the live per-lane state is the packed word count plus three. The packed column table is staged once per block from global memory by a cooperative strided copy followed by one barrier, and is read-only thereafter. Its steady-state access is **not** a broadcast: at each Gray step a lane reads the column bundle indexed by its own flip index, and flip indices differ across lanes, so shared-memory bank behaviour under that scattered read is a measured quantity rather than an assumption.

That register and shared-memory budget is the central occupancy hypothesis of the study. A packed accumulator holds a fixed number of words for any order the mapping supports, where a byte-oriented accumulator grows with $n$ and will reach scratch memory; each block additionally reserves a column table linear in $n$. Whether that budget, instruction scheduling, or the scattered shared-memory read is what limits occupancy is settled by each field's measurements, not by the estimate stated here.

The per-lane budget for the two paths is closer than it looks, which is why this field's comparison turns on the memory hierarchy rather than on registers alone. The bit-sliced path holds three `u64` value planes for any order the mapping supports, so its live per-lane budget is $3 + 3 = 6$ words of 64 bits — 12 registers of 32 bits — and its shared read-only column table is three `u64` per column, or $24n$ bytes per block ($576$ bytes at $n = 24$). The lookup-table control packs one element per nibble, so its accumulator is $\lceil n/16 \rceil$ words — one at $n = 16$, two at $n = 20$ and $n = 24$ — giving a live budget of 4 to 5 words, and its column table is $8n\lceil n/16 \rceil$ bytes per block ($384$ bytes at $n = 24$). Whether the extra register word or the table working set dominates is a measured question.

Both paths stage their column table into the same block-local shared memory. Holding the mapping fixed across them is what makes the later comparison an arithmetic comparison rather than a mapping comparison.

The study's final design must also state whether the three-plane state is a public packed-field representation or a permanent-specialized internal one. title: Runtime qualification of wave utilization and launch duration
description:
A bounded qualification receipt across the study's retained GPU permanent paths: wave utilization, the occupancy-limiting resource, transfer and launch overhead, sustained-kernel duration, and watchdog-safe per-launch work bounds re-derived by measurement.

## Background

A go decision needs to know not only how fast a kernel runs but what the device is doing while it runs, and how long a single launch may safely last. Neither has been measured for any permanent kernel in this repository: no occupancy, register-count, spill, or profiler record for these kernels exists anywhere in the tree.

The watchdog record is contested and has to be treated as such. A prior calibration placed a hang boundary at roughly $190$–$200$ s per launch and derived per-field work budgets on $\text{sub\_batch} \cdot 2^n$ of $4.0 \times 10^9$ at $q = 3$, $1.3 \times 10^9$ at $q = 5$, and $3.5 \times 10^8$ at $q = 7$, with a $400$ ms host cooldown, and recorded that the $\mathbb{F}_3$ kernel never tripped it even on a $2300$ s single launch at $n = 32$. A later observation recorded one device hang and explicitly retracted the attribution of that hang to a watchdog timeout, because no diagnostic separated the possible causes. The safe launch bound reported here therefore comes from this study's own measurement, citing the earlier calibration as a prior rather than as an established device property.

Per-kernel resource figures are produced by each field's own measurement campaign, which reports them against the per-lane register budget and per-block shared-memory allocation that kernel's design predicted. This qualification consumes those committed figures rather than re-measuring them, and adds what no single field can settle: whether that register and shared-memory budget is what limits occupancy across the study's kernels, or whether instruction scheduling, the scattered shared-memory read of the column table, or something else dominates. That is the study's central occupancy hypothesis, and this is where it is answered device-wide.

- [hard] REQ-02: The receipt reports the occupancy-limiting resource for each retained path, together with registers per thread, private scratch memory per thread, shared memory per block, and spill counts; figures already committed by a field's own measurement campaign are cited to their receipt rather than re-measured, and the citation names the file.

- [hard] REQ-04: The receipt states, across the study's kernels, whether the per-lane register budget and per-block shared-memory allocation of the lane-owns-interval mapping is what limits occupancy, naming the resource that does limit it where the answer is no, and citing the measurement behind the verdict.

title: Architecture scope statement with compile evidence
description:
The supported GPU architecture set for the study's prototype kernels, stated explicitly and backed by committed compile evidence for each architecture claimed.

## Background

The architecture scope of the permanent kernels is narrower than the repository's target list suggests. The production kernels are compiled with a single unconditional offload architecture, `gfx1030`. A separate per-architecture code-object pipeline exists and records what compiled through a build manifest consumed by the crate's architecture type, but its only sources today are generated no-op probes, and the generated code-object directory is not tracked in the repository.

A claim of support for an architecture is therefore only as good as the compile evidence behind it. The honest floor for the study is the one architecture its kernels are actually built for; widening that set means adding offload-architecture flags to the prototype crate's build and committing what each build produced.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: The prototype crate's build accepts an explicit set of offload architectures, defaulting to the single architecture the study measured on, so the compiled set is a stated input rather than an incidental one.
- [hard] REQ-02: A committed artifact records, for each architecture in that set, the compiler invocation and its outcome for every prototype kernel the study retained.
- [hard] REQ-03: A committed statement names the supported GPU architecture scope for the study's kernels, and every architecture it names has compile evidence in that artifact.
- [hard] REQ-04: An architecture that fails to compile is recorded with its failure output and excluded from the supported set, rather than dropped silently.
- [hard] REQ-05: The prototype crate's README states the supported architecture set together with the command that regenerates the compile evidence.
- [hard] REQ-06: `cargo build --manifest-path dev/research/permanent_wave_gpu/Cargo.toml --release` passes on a ROCm host for the default architecture set.

## Notes

Scope is compile-time architecture evidence. Runtime behaviour on any architecture beyond the measured one is outside this work, and the statement says so.

The prototype crate sits outside the default Cargo workspace, so the workspace CI pipeline never compiles it; the explicit `--manifest-path` invocation above is the only build evidence for this change.

planning.outcome: The study's supported GPU architecture set is stated, with compile evidence committed for each architecture claimed.

terminal.worker_sized_reason: One build-script flag surface plus a compile sweep over an already-written kernel set is a small self-contained cycle.

footprint.uncertainty: Whether more than gfx1030 can be claimed depends on which offload architectures the study's HIP toolchain compiles the prototype kernels for on the available host.

title: Field-by-field go/no-go synthesis with production design
description:
The study's findings document: a per-field go or no-go verdict grounded in the committed receipts, a production design behind every go, the validity argument for the $\mathbb{F}_3$ Boolean representation, and the decision on where a permanent-specialized representation lives.

## Background

The study concludes per field, and a no-go is a legitimate conclusion where reproducible evidence does not support GPU acceleration. A go decision requires exact equivalence, reproducible receipts, a safe launch duration, and an end-to-end crossover against the best applicable in-tree CPU path; a win on an isolated operator is insufficient.

Three design questions have to be settled in the same document.

The $\mathbb{F}_3$ packed representation encodes a lane as a magnitude bit and a sign bit, with the sign a don't-care when the magnitude is zero. $\mathbb{F}_3$ receives two simultaneous algebraic advantages: $3 = 2^2 - 1$, so Mersenne-style addition is cheap, and $|\mathbb{F}_3^*| = 2$, so the only nonzero distinction is sign. Neither holds for $\mathbb{F}_5^*$ of order four nor for $\mathbb{F}_7^*$ of order six. The document must explain why this is a Boolean encoding of $\mathbb{F}_3$ arithmetic rather than the permanent of a matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$.

A production design converges on the repository's existing device infrastructure rather than growing a parallel one. Persistent device buffers, pinned host buffers, streams, a stream pool, and launch-dimension types already exist and are public in `crates/gf2-kernels-hip/src/host/`; the permanent dispatcher bypasses them today, allocating and freeing per call. The dispatcher also asserts on every device return code and panics, where the repository's accelerator contract requires unsupported capabilities and recoverable resource failures to select a tested fallback while fatal device failures stay explicit.

The representation boundary has exactly two compliant resolutions: change the canonical public packed $\mathbb{F}_7$ representation at its source once broader evidence supports it, or keep the public representation as it is and define the three-plane state as an internal permanent-kernel representation with explicit scope, shared behavioral tests, and a tracked convergence condition. A public packed representation also attracts a proof obligation by repository convention, which an internal permanent-kernel state does not obviously attract.

An archived encoding decision rejected a three-plane $\mathbb{F}_7$ candidate under a workload model weighting each Gray transition as one packed add or subtract plus roughly $n-1$ packed multiplications, and states that a re-benchmark is not a re-decision authority for it. Where this study's receipts support the candidate under the permanent workload, that document is amended at its source with the new evidence rather than silently contradicted.

## Success Criteria

- [hard] REQ-01: A findings document states a go or no-go verdict for each of $\mathbb{F}_3$, $\mathbb{F}_5$, and $\mathbb{F}_7$, each supported by a citation to a committed receipt.
- [hard] REQ-02: Each verdict states the measured crossover condition against the best applicable in-tree CPU path, or states explicitly that no crossover was observed within the measured range.
- [hard] REQ-03: The document specifies the intra-matrix parallel Ryser decomposition the study exercised — the per-lane Gray interval, the per-lane accumulator initialization, the lane-local row-product reduction, and the cross-lane partial-sum reduction — and links the executable prototype implementing it.
- [hard] REQ-04: The document explains why the $\mathbb{F}_3$ Boolean representation is valid for a permanent over $\mathbb{F}_3$ without treating an odd-characteristic permanent as a permanent over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
- [hard] REQ-05: For each of $\mathbb{F}_5$ and $\mathbb{F}_7$, the document reports at least two measured arithmetic representations before selecting or rejecting a design, citing the receipt for each.
- [hard] REQ-06: Every go verdict carries a production design covering input layout; persistent device buffers and streams named as the existing `DeviceBuffer`, `HipStreamPool`, and `LaunchDims` types in `crates/gf2-kernels-hip/src/host/`; bounded-duration launches; per-device initialization; error propagation that selects a tested CPU fallback for unsupported capabilities and recoverable resource failures while leaving fatal device failures explicit; and behavioral-equivalence coverage.
- [hard] REQ-07: The document names the public packed-field representation and the permanent-specialized internal state as distinct surfaces, chooses one of the two compliant resolutions described in the background, and, where the internal state is chosen, records the named exception together with its tracked convergence condition.
- [hard] REQ-08: Where the study's receipts support the three-plane $\mathbb{F}_7$ candidate, the archived $\mathbb{F}_7$ encoding decision document is amended at its source with the permanent-workload evidence and the changed verdict; otherwise the findings document states that the archived decision stands and cites the measurement leaving it standing.
- [hard] REQ-09: Falsified hypotheses, rejected candidates, and censored measurements are recorded together with the evidence contradicting them rather than removed.
- [hard] REQ-10: Every quantitative claim in the document resolves to a committed receipt file or to an in-tree source location.
- [hard] REQ-11: For each of $\mathbb{F}_5$ and $\mathbb{F}_7$, the document states whether the declared scientifically relevant operating point reached at least $1.5\times$ the best applicable in-tree CPU throughput inside the documented safe launch-duration bound, cites the receipt, and records the measured factor and the shortfall where it did not.

## Notes

The document consumes committed evidence and introduces no new measurement.

The archived encoding decision lives under `dev/archive/`, which is permanent repository content; amending it is a deliberate act that needs owner approval before it lands.

Device facts stated in the findings are the receipted ones. Where an in-tree comment disagrees with a receipt — for example a compute-unit count recorded in a test file — the receipt governs and the stale comment is corrected in the same change.

The $\mathbb{F}_3$ arithmetic background is [Scheinerman2024].
